services.name: Amazon EC2
services.oneLiner: Resizable virtual (and bare-metal) servers with the widest choice of CPU, GPU, accelerator, memory and storage shapes on AWS.
whenToUse: Workloads needing OS-level control, custom kernels/agents, licensed software (BYOL, Dedicated Hosts) or long-running processes
Specialized hardware: GPUs (P/G families), Trainium/Inferentia, high-memory (X/U), local NVMe (I/d families), HPC (Hpc families)
Steady-state fleets where Savings Plans/RIs/Spot make per-hour compute the cheapest option
Lift-and-shift migrations (often via Application Migration Service) before modernizing
whenNotToUse: Spiky or event-driven work where Lambda/Fargate remove idle cost and patching
Teams without capacity to own OS patching, AMI pipelines, scaling and hardening
keyFacts: Instance store is ephemeral (lost on stop/terminate/host failure); EBS volumes are AZ-scoped

Purchase options: On-Demand, Savings Plans (up to 72% off), Reserved Instances, Spot (up to 90% off, 2-minute interruption notice), Dedicated Hosts/Instances, Capacity Reservations / Capacity Blocks for ML
Placement groups: cluster (low latency, single AZ), spread (max 7 running instances per AZ per group), partition (up to 7 partitions per AZ)
Graviton (Arm) generally gives the best price-performance; Graviton5 instances (M9g/C9g/R9g, 2026) claim up to 25% better performance than Graviton4
IMDSv2 (session tokens) should be enforced; default vCPU-based On-Demand/Spot quotas per instance family per Region
Status checks: system, instance, attached EBS — plus application status checks (Aug 2026) for app-level failures
services.pricingModel: Per-second billing (Linux/Windows, 60-second minimum) by instance type and purchase option; plus EBS, data transfer out, Elastic IPs (public IPv4 charged hourly since Feb 2024) and licensing.

comparesWith.difference: Lambda is event-driven, per-ms billing, max 15 min per invoke and no server management; EC2 gives full control and long-running processes.
Fargate runs containers without managing instances (per vCPU/GB-second); EC2 is cheaper at high steady utilization and supports GPUs, daemons and host access.
Lightsail bundles a VM, storage, DNS and transfer for a fixed monthly price; EC2 offers full VPC/instance flexibility.

recentLaunches.title: M9g/M9gd instances powered by AWS Graviton5 (C9g and R9g followed)
EC2 application status checks detect app-level failures (e.g. stopped web server)
T8i burstable instances GA — lowest-cost EC2, ~30% better price-performance than T3
Nested virtualization (KVM/Hyper-V) on virtual instances

interviewTips: Be ready to pick an instance family from requirements (memory:vCPU ratio, network bandwidth, local NVMe, GPU) and justify Graviton vs x86
Explain a cost strategy: Savings Plans for baseline, Spot for fault-tolerant/batch, On-Demand for peaks, and Capacity Reservations for DR/ML capacity
Know HA: spread across AZs behind an ELB with an Auto Scaling group; placement groups trade HA for latency

services.name: AWS Lambda
services.oneLiner: Event-driven serverless functions billed per request and per millisecond, now also with durable functions, Managed Instances and MicroVMs.
whenToUse: Event processing from S3, SQS, SNS, EventBridge, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, API Gateway, ALB
Spiky, unpredictable or low-average traffic where scale-to-zero matters
Glue code, automation, lightweight APIs and multi-step workflows (durable functions checkpoint and wait up to 1 year)
whenNotToUse: Single tasks longer than 15 minutes on standard Lambda (use durable functions, Lambda Managed Instances up to 90 min for async/ESM, Fargate or Batch)
Sustained high-throughput compute where per-ms pricing exceeds EC2/Fargate cost, or workloads needing GPUs
Latency-critical paths that cannot tolerate cold starts without SnapStart/provisioned concurrency
keyFacts: Timeout max 900 s (15 min); Lambda Managed Instances allow up to 90 min for async and most event-source-mapping invocations
Memory 128 MB–10,240 MB (CPU scales with memory; 1,769 MB ≈ 1 vCPU); /tmp 512 MB–10,240 MB
Payloads: 6 MB sync request/response, 200 MB streamed response, 1 MB async (raised from 256 KB in Oct 2025)
Default 1,000 concurrent executions per Region (increasable to tens of thousands); each function scales by 1,000 execution environments every 10 s
Package: 50 MB zipped / 250 MB unzipped incl. 5 layers; container images up to 10 GB
Durable functions: up to 3,000 durable operations and 100 MB checkpointed state per execution; waits do not incur compute charges
Network bandwidth 625 Mbps per execution environment by default, up to 3,000 Mbps on request (non-VPC functions)
services.pricingModel: Per request plus GB-seconds of duration (x86 vs Arm rates); provisioned concurrency billed while enabled; Lambda Managed Instances use EC2 instance pricing (Savings Plans/RIs apply) plus a management fee.

comparesWith.difference: Fargate runs long-lived containers without a 15-minute cap and bills per vCPU/GB-second while running; Lambda bills per invocation and scales to zero.
Step Functions orchestrates many services visually with 220+ integrations; Lambda durable functions keep orchestration in code inside one function.
EC2 is cheaper for sustained load and offers any hardware; Lambda removes servers, patching and idle cost.

recentLaunches.title: Lambda durable functions — checkpointed multi-step workflows that can suspend for up to one year
Lambda MicroVMs — Firecracker VM-level isolation, instant launch and up to 8-hour suspension
SnapStart for container images (sub-second starts)
90-minute function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances

interviewTips: Discuss cold-start mitigation: SnapStart, provisioned concurrency, smaller packages, Arm; and reserved concurrency to protect downstreams
Know retries and failure handling per invocation type: async retries twice + destinations/DLQ; SQS partial batch failure reporting; idempotency
Explain when to reach for Lambda Managed Instances (steady high volume, EC2 pricing, specialized instances) vs standard Lambda

services.name: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling
services.oneLiner: Keeps a group of EC2 instances healthy and sized to demand across AZs using target tracking, step, scheduled and predictive scaling.
whenToUse: Stateless web/app tiers behind a load balancer that need self-healing and multi-AZ distribution
Mixed On-Demand/Spot fleets using mixed instances policies with capacity-optimized allocation
Workloads with slow boot times, using warm pools and predictive scaling ahead of daily peaks
whenNotToUse: Stateful singletons (databases) where replacement loses data — use managed databases instead
Container or serverless platforms that already scale for you (ECS services, EKS Karpenter/Auto Mode, Lambda)
keyFacts: Health checks: EC2 status checks by default; enable ELB health checks so unhealthy targets are replaced
Default cooldown 300 s; instance warm-up setting for target tracking; lifecycle hooks (default 1 h timeout) for bootstrap/drain
Rebalances instances evenly across AZs; Capacity Rebalancing proactively replaces Spot instances at elevated interruption risk
Predictive scaling forecasts from up to 14 days of history; warm pools keep pre-initialized stopped/hibernated/running instances
Launch templates required for new features (launch configurations are legacy)
services.pricingModel: No charge for Auto Scaling itself; you pay for the EC2 instances, EBS and CloudWatch alarms/metrics it uses.

comparesWith.difference: EC2 provides the instances; Auto Scaling manages their count, health and AZ distribution.
ELB distributes traffic and reports target health; Auto Scaling adds/removes the targets.

recentLaunches.title: Warm pools support Auto Scaling groups with mixed instances policies
Batch instance termination — up to 100 instance IDs per API call

interviewTips: Pick the metric: target tracking on CPU or ALBRequestCountPerTarget; SQS backlog-per-instance for workers
Explain how to scale in safely: connection draining (deregistration delay), lifecycle hooks, termination policies and scale-in protection

services.name: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
services.oneLiner: PaaS that provisions and manages EC2, Auto Scaling, load balancing and deployments for web apps from uploaded code.
whenToUse: Teams wanting a quick path to run Java, .NET, Node.js, Python, PHP, Ruby, Go or Docker web apps with managed platform updates
Lift-and-shift of traditional web apps where you still want access to the underlying EC2 resources
whenNotToUse: Complex microservice platforms with fine-grained infra needs — use ECS/EKS with IaC
New simple container apps where ECS Express Mode is now the recommended AWS path
keyFacts: Environment tiers: web server and worker (worker pulls from an SQS queue via a daemon)
Deployment policies: all at once, rolling, rolling with additional batch, immutable, traffic splitting; blue/green via CNAME swap
Configuration via .ebextensions and platform hooks; resources are created with CloudFormation in your account
Cluster mode (Sep 2026) deploys multiple applications on shared Amazon EKS infrastructure
services.pricingModel: No additional charge; pay for the underlying EC2, ELB, EBS, RDS and other resources.

comparesWith.difference: ECS (especially Express Mode) is container-native with finer control over tasks and networking; Beanstalk is code-first PaaS over EC2.
App Runner is closed to new customers (Apr 2026); Beanstalk remains open and supports non-container runtimes.

recentLaunches.title: AI-powered environment analysis with troubleshooting recommendations via Bedrock
Cluster mode — managed multi-application deployment on shared EKS infrastructure

interviewTips: Know the deployment policies and which ones avoid downtime or capacity reduction (immutable, traffic splitting, blue/green)
Point out that the RDS instance should be decoupled from the environment lifecycle in production

services.name: Amazon Lightsail
services.oneLiner: Simplified VPS, containers, managed databases and CDN bundled at predictable monthly prices.
whenToUse: Small websites, WordPress/LAMP stacks, dev/test and small business apps with fixed budgets
Users who want a simple console and bundled transfer allowance rather than full VPC design
whenNotToUse: Enterprise workloads needing Auto Scaling, advanced VPC networking, broad instance choice or complex IAM
Workloads that will quickly outgrow bundles (migrate to EC2 via snapshot export)
keyFacts: Bundles include vCPU, memory, SSD storage, and a data transfer allowance; static IPs are free while attached
Can peer with a default VPC in the same Region; snapshots can be exported to EC2
Offers managed databases, load balancers, container services, object storage and CDN distributions
services.pricingModel: Fixed monthly bundle price (hourly pro-rated); overage for data transfer beyond the bundle allowance.

comparesWith.difference: EC2 has full flexibility and elasticity; Lightsail trades flexibility for simplicity and predictable price.

recentLaunches.title: OpenClaw on Lightsail to run private autonomous AI agents

interviewTips: Mention Lightsail only when the customer is small/simple; show the migration path to EC2 as they grow

services.name: AWS Batch
services.oneLiner: Managed job scheduler that queues containerized batch jobs and provisions EC2, Spot, Fargate or EKS capacity to run them.
whenToUse: Large numbers of independent jobs (rendering, genomics, simulations, ETL) with queueing and priorities
Array jobs and multi-node parallel (MPI) HPC jobs; ML training via Batch on EKS
Cost-optimized Spot-heavy compute environments with retry strategies
whenNotToUse: Low-latency request/response services
Simple event-driven tasks under 15 minutes that Lambda handles more cheaply
keyFacts: Concepts: job definitions, job queues (with priority), compute environments (managed or unmanaged; EC2, Spot, Fargate, EKS)
Array jobs up to 10,000 child jobs; multi-node parallel jobs span multiple EC2 instances
Fair-share scheduling policies share capacity across users/teams
Allocation strategies such as SPOT_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED / SPOT_PRICE_CAPACITY_OPTIMIZED reduce interruptions
services.pricingModel: No additional charge; pay for EC2/Fargate/EKS resources consumed by jobs.

comparesWith.difference: Step Functions orchestrates workflow steps (can submit Batch jobs); Batch schedules and runs the compute.
Lambda suits short event handlers; Batch suits long, heavy or HPC jobs with queues.

interviewTips: Design a Spot-first Batch environment with retries and checkpointing for fault tolerance
Contrast Batch with ParallelCluster for tightly coupled HPC needing Slurm and EFA

services.name: AWS Outposts
services.oneLiner: AWS-managed racks and servers that run EC2, EBS, S3 on Outposts, ECS/EKS, RDS and more in your own data center.
whenToUse: Low-latency access to on-prem systems, local data processing, or data residency where no Region/Local Zone fits
Hybrid apps needing the same AWS APIs, tooling and control plane on premises
Edge compute for new customers now that Snowball Edge is closed to new customers
whenNotToUse: Workloads that can run in a Region or Local Zone (cheaper and elastic)
Sites without reliable connectivity to the parent Region (the control plane lives in the Region)
keyFacts: Racks (42U) and 1U/2U servers; capacity is fixed — you size and order it ahead (3-year term)
Connected to a parent Region via a service link; requires connectivity for management
Local gateway (LGW) routes to on-prem networks; subnets extend a Region VPC onto the Outpost
Second-generation single-rack model (Sep 2026) offers up to 2,688 vCPUs
services.pricingModel: 3-year term with all/partial/no upfront payment covering hardware, installation, maintenance and software; data transfer and some services billed separately.

comparesWith.difference: Local Zones are AWS-owned metro extensions of a Region; Outposts sits in your facility.
Snowball Edge is portable/disconnected edge but closed to new customers since Nov 2025; Outposts is permanently installed and connected.

recentLaunches.title: Self-service lifecycle management: configure, quote, order and renew Outposts
Second-generation single-rack Outposts with up to 2,688 vCPUs

interviewTips: Call out that Outposts availability depends on the service link and local capacity planning — design for N+1 and a Region DR path

services.name: AWS Local Zones
services.oneLiner: AWS infrastructure in metro areas, attached to a parent Region, for single-digit-millisecond latency and local data residency.
whenToUse: Latency-sensitive apps near end users: media rendering, real-time gaming, live video, hybrid migrations
Data residency requirements in a country/metro without a full Region
whenNotToUse: Workloads needing the full service catalogue (only a subset — EC2, EBS, ECS, EKS, ALB, Direct Connect, etc. — is available)
When the parent Region already meets latency needs
keyFacts: Opt-in per zone; you extend a VPC by creating subnets in the Local Zone
Services are a subset of the parent Region and vary by zone; instance types are limited
New zones in 2026 include Istanbul, Hanoi, Athens and Las Vegas
services.pricingModel: Pay per resource at Local Zone rates (typically higher than the parent Region), plus data transfer.

comparesWith.difference: Wavelength embeds compute inside telco 5G networks for mobile-edge latency; Local Zones serve metro areas over the internet/Direct Connect.
Outposts runs in your data center; Local Zones are AWS-operated.

recentLaunches.title: Local Zone in Istanbul, Türkiye
Local Zone in Hanoi, Vietnam (with S3 and EBS Local Snapshots)
Local Zone in Athens, Greece
Local Zone in Las Vegas, Nevada

interviewTips: Differentiate Region vs AZ vs Local Zone vs Wavelength vs Outposts on latency, service breadth and who owns the facility

services.name: AWS Wavelength
services.oneLiner: AWS compute and storage embedded in telecom carriers' 5G networks for ultra-low-latency mobile edge applications.
whenToUse: Mobile/connected-device apps needing very low latency to 5G users: AR/VR, connected vehicles, live video analytics
Edge inference or media processing where traffic should stay inside the carrier network instead of traversing the internet
whenNotToUse: General internet-facing apps (use a Region, Local Zone or CloudFront)
Users not on the partner carrier network
keyFacts: Wavelength Zones are tied to a carrier (e.g. Verizon, Vodafone, KDDI, SK Telecom, Bell) and a parent Region
Carrier gateway provides connectivity to the carrier network; extend a VPC with a Wavelength subnet
Limited service set: EC2, EBS, ECS, EKS and a few others
services.pricingModel: Pay for instances and storage at Wavelength rates plus data transfer.

comparesWith.difference: Local Zones are metro-area extensions for any user; Wavelength is inside a specific 5G carrier network.

interviewTips: Only propose Wavelength when latency to mobile 5G clients is the key requirement

services.name: AWS App Runner (closed to new customers)
services.oneLiner: Fully managed web app/container service — in maintenance: closed to new customers since April 30, 2026; ECS Express Mode is the recommended replacement.
whenToUse: Existing App Runner customers running simple HTTP services from source or container image
Existing customers can still create new services; AWS keeps security/availability investment but no new features
whenNotToUse: Any new customer or greenfield design — use Amazon ECS Express Mode (Fargate + ALB + auto scaling in one call)
Workloads needing VPC-first networking control, sidecars or non-HTTP protocols
keyFacts: Availability change announced Mar 31, 2026; no longer accessible to new customers from Apr 30, 2026
Migration path: blue/green to ECS Express Mode using Route 53 weighted records
Scales on concurrent requests per instance; can scale to a provisioned (idle memory-only billed) minimum
services.pricingModel: Per vCPU-second and GB-second for active instances, memory-only charge for provisioned idle instances, plus build minutes.

comparesWith.difference: ECS Express Mode is the recommended successor and has no extra charge beyond the Fargate/ALB resources it creates.
Beanstalk is still open to new customers and supports non-container runtimes on EC2.

recentLaunches.title: App Runner moves to maintenance; closed to new customers from Apr 30, 2026

interviewTips: If an interviewer mentions App Runner, show currency: it is closed to new customers — recommend ECS Express Mode and explain the migration

services.name: Amazon ECS
services.oneLiner: AWS-native container orchestrator running tasks and services on Fargate, ECS Managed Instances or self-managed EC2.
whenToUse: Containerized microservices where you want AWS-integrated simplicity without Kubernetes overhead
Simple web apps via ECS Express Mode (one call provisions Fargate service, ALB, auto scaling, networking and URL)
Mixed launch types: Fargate for simplicity, ECS Managed Instances/EC2 for GPUs, Spot or specific instance types
whenNotToUse: Teams standardized on Kubernetes APIs, Helm and CNCF tooling or needing multi-cloud portability (use EKS)
Short event handlers better served by Lambda
keyFacts: Constructs: cluster, task definition (up to 10 containers), task, service, capacity providers
Networking: awsvpc mode gives each task its own ENI and security group; Service Connect/VPC Lattice for service-to-service
Deployments: rolling, built-in blue/green, linear and canary (NLB support added Feb 2026); circuit breaker auto-rollback
IAM: task execution role (pull image, logs) vs task role (app permissions)
ECS Managed Instances: AWS-managed EC2 capacity incl. GPUs, Trainium/Inferentia and Spot
services.pricingModel: No charge for the control plane or Express Mode; pay for Fargate vCPU/GB-seconds or EC2 instances (Managed Instances adds a management fee).

comparesWith.difference: EKS is upstream Kubernetes ($0.10/hour per cluster standard support) with the CNCF ecosystem; ECS is simpler and AWS-opinionated.
App Runner is closed to new customers; ECS Express Mode is its replacement.
Fargate is a compute engine ECS (and EKS) can use; ECS is the orchestrator.

recentLaunches.title: ECS Express Mode — production-ready app stack from a container image in one step
NLB support for linear and canary deployments
20-second high-resolution metrics for faster service auto scaling
Up to 60% lower GPU management fees for ECS Managed Instances and EKS Auto Mode

interviewTips: Explain ECS vs EKS as a people/operability decision, not only a technical one
Know the two IAM roles and how secrets are injected from Secrets Manager/SSM Parameter Store

services.name: Amazon EKS
services.oneLiner: Managed, conformant Kubernetes control plane with options from self-managed nodes to fully managed EKS Auto Mode and EKS Capabilities.
whenToUse: Organizations standardized on Kubernetes, Helm, operators and GitOps, or needing portability/hybrid (EKS Hybrid Nodes, EKS Anywhere)
Large multi-tenant platforms and ML platforms (GPU/Trainium node pools, Karpenter, Ray)
whenNotToUse: Small teams without Kubernetes skills and a few services — ECS is simpler
Pure event-driven functions (Lambda)
keyFacts: Control plane spans 3 AZs; standard support ~14 months per Kubernetes version, extended support +12 months at higher price
Pricing: $0.10 per cluster-hour (standard support), $0.60 in extended support; Provisioned Control Plane tiers for scale
Provisioned Control Plane clusters have a 99.99% SLA and an 8XL tier (Mar 2026); version rollbacks within 7 days (Jun 2026)
EKS Auto Mode manages nodes, Karpenter scaling, load balancing, storage and networking add-ons
EKS Capabilities (Nov 2025): managed Argo CD, AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK) and kro, running in AWS-owned accounts
Pod identity: EKS Pod Identity (preferred) or IRSA; VPC CNI assigns VPC IPs to pods (prefix delegation for density)
services.pricingModel: Per cluster-hour for the control plane plus EC2/Fargate/Auto Mode compute (Auto Mode adds a per-instance management fee); EKS Capabilities are billed separately per enabled capability.

comparesWith.difference: ECS has no control-plane fee and fewer moving parts; EKS offers Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem.
Fargate can run EKS pods serverlessly (no DaemonSets, no GPUs); Auto Mode is the more complete managed-node option.

recentLaunches.title: EKS Capabilities: managed Argo CD, ACK and kro
99.99% SLA and new 8XL scaling tier for Provisioned Control Plane
Kubernetes version rollbacks within seven days
Kubernetes 1.36 support

interviewTips: Be ready to discuss multi-tenancy (namespaces vs clusters), IP exhaustion (prefix delegation, secondary CIDRs, IPv6) and upgrade strategy
Contrast Karpenter/Auto Mode with Cluster Autoscaler and managed node groups

services.name: AWS Fargate
services.oneLiner: Serverless compute engine for ECS tasks and EKS pods — no instances to provision, patch or scale.
whenToUse: Containers where you want per-task isolation and no node management
Variable workloads and batch tasks; Fargate Spot for interruption-tolerant tasks (up to 70% off)
whenNotToUse: GPU workloads, privileged containers, DaemonSets or host-level access
Very high steady utilization where EC2/Managed Instances with Savings Plans is cheaper
keyFacts: Task sizes up to 16 vCPU and 120 GB memory; ephemeral storage 20 GiB default, up to 200 GiB
Each task gets its own ENI (awsvpc) and a dedicated kernel/micro-VM boundary
Linux x86_64 and ARM64 (Graviton) and Windows containers on ECS
Fargate Spot gives a 2-minute SIGTERM warning; custom STOPSIGNAL supported since Dec 2025
Compute Savings Plans apply to Fargate
services.pricingModel: Per-second billing (1-minute minimum) for vCPU, memory, OS/architecture and extra ephemeral storage.

comparesWith.difference: Lambda is per-invocation with a 15-minute limit; Fargate runs long-lived containers billed while running.
EC2 gives cheaper steady capacity and GPUs but requires node management.

recentLaunches.title: Custom container stop signals on Fargate for graceful shutdown
tmpfs mounts for Linux tasks on Fargate and ECS Managed Instances

interviewTips: Know Fargate limitations (no GPUs, no DaemonSets on EKS) and when to switch to ECS Managed Instances or EKS Auto Mode

services.name: Amazon ECR
services.oneLiner: Managed OCI container image and artifact registry with scanning, replication, pull-through cache and signing.
whenToUse: Storing private images for ECS, EKS, Lambda and SageMaker with IAM-based access
Cross-Region/cross-account replication for multi-Region deployments; pull-through cache for Docker Hub/other upstreams
whenNotToUse: Non-OCI package types (use CodeArtifact for npm/Maven/PyPI)
keyFacts: Image scanning: basic and enhanced (Amazon Inspector, continuous CVE scanning)
Lifecycle policies expire old/untagged images; tag immutability prevents overwrites
Encryption at rest with AES-256 or KMS; VPC interface endpoints (plus S3 gateway endpoint for layers)
Pull-through cache syncs OCI signatures and SBOM referrers (Apr 2026); managed image signing and an archive storage class (Nov 2025)
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month stored plus data transfer out; enhanced scanning billed via Inspector.

comparesWith.difference: CodeBuild builds and pushes images; ECR stores and scans them.

recentLaunches.title: Managed container image signing and archive storage class
Pull-through cache supports referrer discovery and syncing of signatures and SBOMs

interviewTips: For private subnets, remember ECR needs interface endpoints for api/dkr and the S3 gateway endpoint for image layers

services.name: Amazon S3
services.oneLiner: Regional object storage with 11 nines durability, strong consistency and storage classes from Standard to Glacier Deep Archive — plus S3 Vectors, S3 Tables and S3 Files.
whenToUse: Data lakes, backups, static assets, logs, ML datasets and any unstructured data at any scale
Static website/SPA origin behind CloudFront (with Origin Access Control)
Vector storage for RAG at low cost (S3 Vectors) and file-system access to bucket data (S3 Files)
whenNotToUse: Low-latency block storage for databases/OS volumes (EBS) or POSIX file locking workloads that need EFS/FSx semantics
Many tiny, frequently updated records better held in DynamoDB
keyFacts: Max object size 50 TB (raised from 5 TB in Dec 2025); single PUT up to 5 GB; multipart up to 10,000 parts
Durability 99.999999999% (11 nines); Standard availability design 99.99%; One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ
Strong read-after-write consistency for all PUT/DELETE/LIST since Dec 2020
Performance: at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix
Storage classes: Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA, One Zone-IA, Express One Zone (single-digit ms), Glacier Instant/Flexible Retrieval, Glacier Deep Archive (12–48 h restore)
Block Public Access and SSE-S3 encryption are on by default for new buckets; ACLs disabled by default (Object Ownership)
S3 Vectors (GA Dec 2025): up to 2 billion vectors per index, 20 trillion per bucket, ~100 ms warm queries, up to 90% cheaper than dedicated vector DBs
Replication: CRR/SRR, Replication Time Control (15-minute SLA for 99.99% of objects); Object Lock for WORM (governance/compliance modes)
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month by storage class, per request (PUT/GET tiers), retrieval fees for IA/Glacier classes, minimum storage durations, data transfer out, and features (replication, Inventory, Storage Lens advanced, S3 Vectors storage/query).

comparesWith.difference: EFS is a POSIX NFS file system mounted by many clients; S3 is object storage via API (S3 Files adds file access to buckets).
EBS is AZ-scoped block storage attached to one instance (Multi-Attach for io1/io2); S3 is Regional object storage.
S3 Tables are table buckets optimized for Apache Iceberg with automatic compaction; general purpose buckets store any objects.

recentLaunches.title: Maximum object size increased to 50 TB
Account regional namespaces for general purpose buckets
Amazon S3 Files — access S3 buckets as shared file systems (built on EFS)
Same-day lifecycle transitions to Standard-IA and One Zone-IA (30-day minimum removed)

interviewTips: Design lifecycle policies across storage classes with minimum durations and retrieval costs in mind
Secure buckets: Block Public Access, bucket policies with aws:SourceVpce / aws:PrincipalOrgID, SSE-KMS with bucket keys, OAC for CloudFront
Know prefix-based request scaling and when to use Express One Zone or S3 Transfer Acceleration

services.name: Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes (legacy Glacier vault service closed to new customers)
services.oneLiner: Low-cost archive storage classes inside S3; the original vault-based Amazon Glacier API stopped accepting new customers on Dec 15, 2025.
whenToUse: Long-term archives, compliance retention and backups accessed rarely (use S3 Glacier Instant/Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive storage classes)
Tape replacement with S3 Object Lock for WORM retention
whenNotToUse: New designs on the legacy vault API — it is in maintenance; use S3 storage classes
Frequently accessed data where retrieval fees and minimum durations dominate cost
keyFacts: Glacier Instant Retrieval: millisecond access, 90-day minimum; Flexible Retrieval: minutes–12 h (expedited 1–5 min), 90-day minimum; Deep Archive: 12–48 h, 180-day minimum
Same 11 nines durability as S3; data stored across at least 3 AZs
Legacy Amazon Glacier (vaults, Vault Lock) closed to new customers from Dec 15, 2025; existing data remains accessible indefinitely
S3 Glacier Select was retired to new customers in 2024; restore objects then query with Athena
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month (lowest of any S3 class for Deep Archive), per-request and per-GB retrieval fees by speed tier, plus early-deletion charges for minimum storage duration.

comparesWith.difference: Glacier classes are S3 storage classes chosen via lifecycle rules; Standard/IA classes give immediate access without restore.
AWS Backup manages backup policies and cold-tier transitions; Glacier classes are the raw archive storage.

recentLaunches.title: Legacy Amazon Glacier vault service moves to maintenance (no new customers from Dec 15, 2025)

interviewTips: Always name the S3 Glacier storage classes, not the legacy vault API, for new architectures
Compute total cost: storage + retrieval + early deletion + request fees for small objects (40 KB overhead per archived object)

services.name: Amazon EBS
services.oneLiner: AZ-scoped, persistent block storage volumes for EC2 with SSD (gp3, io2 Block Express) and HDD (st1, sc1) types.
whenToUse: Boot volumes and databases on EC2 needing low-latency block I/O
Transactional workloads requiring provisioned IOPS (io2 Block Express, sub-millisecond latency)
whenNotToUse: Shared file access across many instances/AZs (use EFS/FSx)
Cross-AZ durability without snapshots/replication — a volume lives in one AZ
keyFacts: gp3: up to 64 TiB, 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s (raised Sep 2025); 3,000 IOPS/125 MiB/s baseline included
io2 Block Express: up to 64 TiB, 256,000 IOPS, 4,000 MiB/s, 99.999% durability; Multi-Attach for io1/io2
Snapshots are incremental and stored in S3 (Regional); Fast Snapshot Restore removes initialization latency
Volumes are replicated within their AZ; annual failure rate 0.1–0.2% for gp/io1, 0.001% for io2
Encryption with KMS (can enable account-level encryption by default); Elastic Volumes change size/type online
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month provisioned by volume type, plus provisioned IOPS/throughput above baseline (gp3, io1/io2), snapshot storage per GB-month and Fast Snapshot Restore hours.

comparesWith.difference: EFS is multi-AZ shared NFS that scales automatically; EBS is single-AZ block storage for one instance.
FSx provides managed Windows/Lustre/ONTAP/OpenZFS file systems; EBS is raw block storage.

recentLaunches.title: gp3 volumes up to 64 TiB, 80,000 IOPS and 2,000 MiB/s
EBS Volume Clones across AWS accounts with re-encryption

interviewTips: Migrate gp2 to gp3 for ~20% lower cost and decoupled performance
Remember instance-level EBS bandwidth limits can cap volume performance

services.name: Amazon EFS
services.oneLiner: Serverless, elastic NFSv4.1 file system shared across thousands of Linux clients and AZs.
whenToUse: Shared file storage for Linux containers (ECS/EKS/Fargate), Lambda, web content, home directories, CI caches
Lift-and-shift apps needing POSIX semantics and multi-AZ availability
whenNotToUse: Windows SMB workloads (use FSx for Windows File Server)
Extreme HPC throughput with sub-ms latency (FSx for Lustre) or lowest-cost bulk storage (S3)
keyFacts: Regional (multi-AZ) and One Zone file systems; 11 nines durability (Regional)
Throughput modes: Elastic (recommended), Provisioned, Bursting
Storage classes: Standard, Infrequent Access, Archive with lifecycle management
Access points enforce POSIX identity and root directories per application; EFS Replication for DR (cross-account supported)
Encryption at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS via EFS mount helper)
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month by storage class, per-GB data access for IA/Archive and Elastic throughput reads/writes, provisioned throughput if used.

comparesWith.difference: FSx offers Windows/SMB, Lustre, ONTAP and OpenZFS with specialized features; EFS is simple elastic NFS.
S3 is cheaper object storage via API; S3 Files (built on EFS) now exposes buckets as file systems.

recentLaunches.title: Amazon S3 Files, built on EFS, brings file-system access to S3 buckets
DataSync Enhanced mode supports EFS as source/destination

interviewTips: Contrast EFS vs EBS vs S3 on sharing, scope (AZ vs Region), latency and cost

services.name: Amazon FSx
services.oneLiner: Fully managed third-party file systems: FSx for Windows File Server, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS.
whenToUse: Windows SMB shares with Active Directory integration, DFS and shadow copies (FSx for Windows)
HPC/ML training needing hundreds of GB/s and sub-ms latency, linked to S3 (FSx for Lustre)
Enterprise NAS migrations needing multiprotocol NFS/SMB/iSCSI, SnapMirror, dedupe (FSx for NetApp ONTAP)
whenNotToUse: Simple elastic Linux NFS shares (EFS is simpler)
Object storage use cases (S3)
keyFacts: Windows and ONTAP support Multi-AZ deployments; Lustre offers scratch (no replication) and persistent deployment types
FSx for Lustre integrates with S3 data repositories (lazy load / export)
FSx for ONTAP can be accessed through S3 APIs (Dec 2025) and supports SnapMirror replication
Amazon FSx File Gateway has been in maintenance since Oct 2024 (use FSx for Windows directly)
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month of provisioned SSD/HDD storage, provisioned throughput (and IOPS for some), backups per GB-month; ONTAP/OpenZFS also charge for capacity-pool tiering.

comparesWith.difference: EFS is serverless NFS with pay-per-use; FSx provisions capacity for specialized file systems.
Storage Gateway caches cloud storage on-prem; FSx is the managed file system in AWS.

recentLaunches.title: FSx for NetApp ONTAP integrates with Amazon S3 for data access
DataSync Enhanced mode supports FSx for Lustre

interviewTips: Map requirement to flavor: SMB+AD → Windows; HPC+S3 → Lustre; NetApp features/multiprotocol → ONTAP; ZFS snapshots/NFS → OpenZFS

services.name: AWS Storage Gateway
services.oneLiner: Hybrid storage appliance (VM or hardware) that gives on-prem apps NFS/SMB, iSCSI and virtual-tape access to AWS storage with local caching.
whenToUse: On-prem apps needing file shares backed by S3 (S3 File Gateway)
Replacing physical tape with virtual tapes in S3/Glacier (Tape Gateway)
Block volumes with cloud-backed snapshots (Volume Gateway cached/stored modes)
whenNotToUse: One-time bulk migration (DataSync is purpose-built)
Windows shares that can live fully in AWS (FSx for Windows; FSx File Gateway is in maintenance)
keyFacts: Gateway types: S3 File, Tape, Volume (FSx File Gateway closed to new customers since Oct 2024)
Deployed as VMware/Hyper-V/KVM VM, EC2 instance or hardware appliance; local cache for low-latency access
Tape Gateway integrates with major backup software and archives to Glacier Flexible Retrieval/Deep Archive
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month of storage in AWS, per-GB data written (capped monthly), request/retrieval fees; hardware appliance purchased separately.

comparesWith.difference: DataSync moves data in bulk/scheduled transfers; Storage Gateway provides ongoing hybrid access with caching.
FSx hosts the file system in AWS; Storage Gateway fronts AWS storage from on-prem.

interviewTips: Pick the gateway type from protocol: NFS/SMB → S3 File, iSCSI → Volume, VTL → Tape

services.name: AWS Backup
services.oneLiner: Centralized, policy-based backup across AWS services and accounts with cross-Region/cross-account copies and immutable vaults.
whenToUse: Org-wide backup policies (via AWS Organizations) for EC2, EBS, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, FSx, S3, EKS and more
Ransomware resilience with Vault Lock and logically air-gapped vaults
Compliance reporting with Backup Audit Manager
whenNotToUse: Continuous replication/low-RPO DR (use Elastic Disaster Recovery, Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables)
keyFacts: Backup plans define frequency, retention, lifecycle to cold storage (90-day minimum in cold) and copy rules
Vault Lock (governance/compliance modes) makes recovery points immutable; logically air-gapped vaults are shareable via AWS RAM
Supports point-in-time restore for RDS, Aurora, S3 and others
Restore testing automates periodic restore validation
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month of backup storage (warm/cold) by resource type, restore per GB, cross-Region transfer, and audit/restore-testing fees.

comparesWith.difference: Glacier classes are storage tiers; Backup is the policy/orchestration layer with cataloged recovery points.

recentLaunches.title: Up to 10x faster Amazon EKS cluster backups
Direct read-only access to S3 backup data via access points without restore
Protect more than 1,000 S3 buckets per account

interviewTips: Discuss a ransomware strategy: separate backup account, Vault Lock compliance mode, air-gapped vault, restore testing

services.name: Amazon S3 Tables
services.oneLiner: Table buckets purpose-built for Apache Iceberg with automatic compaction, snapshot management and higher query throughput.
whenToUse: Analytics tables queried by Athena, Redshift, EMR, Glue, Spark or third-party Iceberg engines
Streaming or frequently updated tabular data needing managed compaction
whenNotToUse: Unstructured objects or non-Iceberg formats (use general purpose buckets)
OLTP access patterns (use a database)
keyFacts: Tables are first-class AWS resources with table-level IAM permissions and namespaces
AWS claims up to 3x faster query performance and up to 10x higher TPS vs self-managed Iceberg tables in general purpose buckets
Integrates with the Glue Data Catalog / Lake Formation and SageMaker Unified Studio
Supports replication and Intelligent-Tiering (Dec 2025) and Iceberg v3 features such as the variant type (Jul 2026)
services.pricingModel: Per GB-month storage, per request, per object monitored, and compaction per object/GB processed.

comparesWith.difference: General purpose buckets hold any object; table buckets add Iceberg-aware maintenance and table-level access control.
Lake Formation governs fine-grained access; S3 Tables stores and maintains the tables.

recentLaunches.title: Replication support and Intelligent-Tiering for S3 Tables
Variant data type support for Apache Iceberg v3 tables

interviewTips: Explain why Iceberg needs compaction/snapshot expiry and how S3 Tables removes that ops burden

services.name: Amazon RDS
services.oneLiner: Managed relational databases for MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2 with automated backups, patching and Multi-AZ.
whenToUse: Lift-and-shift of relational workloads, commercial engines (Oracle, SQL Server, Db2) and licensing (BYOL/License Included)
Standard OLTP where Aurora features are not required or engine versions/extensions must match on-prem
whenNotToUse: Massive horizontal write scale or single-digit-ms key-value access at any scale (DynamoDB)
Multi-Region active-active strongly consistent SQL (Aurora DSQL)
Needing OS access for custom agents — RDS Custom for SQL Server (RDS Custom for Oracle is entering sunset)
keyFacts: Storage up to 64 TiB for MySQL/PostgreSQL/MariaDB (gp3/io2); RDS for Oracle and SQL Server can scale further with additional storage volumes (re:Invent 2025)
Multi-AZ instance: synchronous standby, failover typically 60–120 s; Multi-AZ DB cluster (MySQL/PostgreSQL): 2 readable standbys, failover typically under 35 s
Read replicas: up to 15 (MySQL/MariaDB/PostgreSQL), asynchronous, cross-Region supported
Automated backups retained 0–35 days with point-in-time restore (~5-minute RPO); manual snapshots kept until deleted
RDS Proxy pools connections (important for Lambda) and reduces failover time
Encryption at rest must be chosen at creation (encrypt an unencrypted DB via snapshot copy)
services.pricingModel: Per instance-hour (On-Demand or Reserved; Database Savings Plans since Dec 2025) plus provisioned storage/IOPS, backup storage beyond DB size, data transfer; licence-included pricing for commercial engines.

comparesWith.difference: Aurora decouples storage (6 copies across 3 AZs, up to 256 TiB), faster failover and up to 15 low-lag replicas; RDS is closer to the stock engine.
DynamoDB is serverless NoSQL with predictable latency at any scale; RDS offers joins, SQL and transactions across tables.

recentLaunches.title: RDS for Oracle and SQL Server add capabilities to improve performance and cost (incl. larger storage and Developer Edition options)
RDS for SQL Server supports Bring Your Own Media (License Mobility)
RDS Custom for Oracle enters sunset

interviewTips: Distinguish HA (Multi-AZ) from read scaling (read replicas) from DR (cross-Region replicas / snapshots copy)
Explain how to upgrade major versions with minimal downtime (Blue/Green Deployments)

services.name: Amazon Aurora
services.oneLiner: MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible cloud-native relational database with distributed storage, Serverless v2, Global Database and Limitless scaling.
whenToUse: High-throughput OLTP needing fast failover, many read replicas and auto-growing storage
Variable workloads with Aurora Serverless v2 (scales in fine-grained ACUs, can scale to 0)
Cross-Region DR/low-latency reads via Global Database (typically <1 s replication lag, managed failover)
whenNotToUse: Commercial engines (Oracle/SQL Server) — use RDS
Active-active multi-Region writes with strong consistency (Aurora DSQL or DynamoDB global tables MRSC)
keyFacts: Storage auto-grows in 10 GiB increments up to 256 TiB (doubled from 128 TiB in Jul 2025); 6 copies across 3 AZs, tolerates loss of 2 copies for writes and 3 for reads
Up to 15 Aurora Replicas sharing the storage volume; failover typically ~30 s or less
Global Database: up to 10 secondary Regions (was 5), RPO ~1 s, RTO < 1 minute for managed failover
Aurora PostgreSQL Limitless Database shards horizontally beyond a single writer
I/O-Optimized configuration removes per-I/O charges when I/O > ~25% of spend
New clusters are encrypted at rest by default (Feb 2026)
services.pricingModel: Instances per hour (or Serverless v2 per ACU-hour), storage per GB-month, I/O per million requests (Standard) or none (I/O-Optimized), backups, Global Database replicated writes; Database Savings Plans apply.

comparesWith.difference: RDS supports more engines and exact community versions; Aurora gives better availability, replicas and storage scaling.
Aurora DSQL is serverless, distributed, active-active multi-Region with optimistic concurrency but a PostgreSQL subset; Aurora is single-writer per cluster.

recentLaunches.title: Aurora MySQL and PostgreSQL support up to 256 TiB storage
Server-side encryption at rest by default for all new clusters
Aurora Serverless enhancements with up to 30% better performance and smarter scaling

interviewTips: Explain the quorum storage model (4/6 writes, 3/6 reads) and why failover is fast
Use cluster, reader and custom endpoints appropriately; RDS Proxy for connection storms

services.name: Amazon Aurora DSQL
services.oneLiner: Serverless, distributed PostgreSQL-compatible SQL database with active-active multi-Region strong consistency (GA May 2025).
whenToUse: Globally distributed apps needing multi-Region writes with strong consistency and no failover orchestration
Spiky or unpredictable SQL workloads that want zero infrastructure management and scale-to-zero cost
whenNotToUse: Apps depending on PostgreSQL features DSQL does not support (e.g. foreign keys, some extensions, triggers, sequences historically) or long-running transactions
High-contention write hotspots — optimistic concurrency control causes retries
keyFacts: Availability design: 99.99% single-Region, 99.999% multi-Region
Multi-Region clusters: two peered Regions plus a witness Region; synchronous commit across Regions
Optimistic concurrency control; transactions have size/row and duration limits (5-minute max transaction)
IAM authentication with short-lived tokens; storage up to 256 TiB (Nov 2025)
CDC to Kinesis is GA (Jul 2026)
services.pricingModel: Serverless: Distributed Processing Units (DPUs) for reads/writes/compute plus storage per GB-month; free tier available; Database Savings Plans apply.

comparesWith.difference: Aurora has full PostgreSQL/MySQL compatibility with a single writer; DSQL trades features for active-active scale.
DynamoDB global tables (MREC or MRSC) are NoSQL; DSQL offers SQL with multi-Region strong consistency.

recentLaunches.title: Clusters support up to 256 TiB storage; new connectors and statement-level cost estimates
Cluster creation in seconds and console query editor
Change data capture (CDC) streaming to Kinesis generally available

interviewTips: Explain OCC and why you must build retry logic and avoid hot rows
Contrast DSQL with Aurora Global Database (async, single write Region) for multi-Region designs

services.name: Amazon DynamoDB
services.oneLiner: Serverless key-value and document NoSQL database with single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale, global tables and now native vector search.
whenToUse: High-scale OLTP with known access patterns: user profiles, carts, sessions, gaming, IoT metadata
Serverless apps (pairs with Lambda/API Gateway), event-driven designs with Streams
Multi-Region active-active with global tables (eventual or strong consistency)
whenNotToUse: Ad-hoc relational queries, complex joins or analytics (use Aurora/Redshift/Athena)
Items larger than 400 KB (store in S3 with a pointer)
keyFacts: Max item size 400 KB; partition throughput 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU per partition (adaptive capacity and split-for-heat mitigate hot keys)
Default quotas: 40,000 RCU/WCU per table (increasable), 2,500 tables per Region, 20 GSIs and 5 LSIs per table (LSI limits item collection to 10 GB)
Capacity modes: on-demand (default recommendation) or provisioned with auto scaling; warm throughput to pre-warm
Transactions: up to 100 items / 4 MB per TransactWriteItems; Query/Scan return max 1 MB per page
Global tables: MREC (async, last-writer-wins) or MRSC (strong consistency, GA Jun 2025); multi-account replication (Feb 2026)
PITR restores to any second in the last 1–35 days; Streams retain 24 hours
Vector search (Aug 2026): up to 5 vector indexes per table, 4,096 dimensions, TopK ≤ 100
services.pricingModel: On-demand: per million read/write request units; provisioned: per RCU/WCU-hour (reserved capacity available); plus storage per GB-month (Standard or Standard-IA table class), backups, PITR, global table replicated writes, Streams reads.

comparesWith.difference: Aurora gives SQL, joins and flexible queries; DynamoDB gives predictable latency and near-unlimited scale for known access patterns.
ElastiCache is an in-memory cache (microsecond reads, not primarily durable); DynamoDB is durable with DAX for microsecond caching.
Keyspaces offers the Cassandra (CQL) API; DynamoDB has its own API and richer AWS integrations.

recentLaunches.title: Multi-Region strong consistency global tables integrate with AWS Fault Injection Service
Global tables support multi-account replication
Native vector search — store and query embeddings alongside items

interviewTips: Design keys from access patterns first; single-table design, GSIs overloading, write sharding for hot partitions
Know strongly consistent vs eventually consistent reads (RCU cost 1 vs 0.5 per 4 KB) and that GSIs are always eventually consistent

services.name: Amazon ElastiCache
services.oneLiner: Managed in-memory caching with Valkey, Redis OSS and Memcached, available serverless or node-based.
whenToUse: Caching database queries/sessions to cut latency (sub-millisecond) and database load
Leaderboards, rate limiting, pub/sub, and ephemeral queues with Valkey/Redis data structures
whenNotToUse: Primary durable database of record (use MemoryDB for durable Redis-compatible storage)
Large datasets rarely re-read — caching adds cost without hit rate
keyFacts: Engines: Valkey (recommended; ~20–33% lower price than Redis OSS), Redis OSS, Memcached
Serverless: scales automatically, pay per GB-hour stored and ElastiCache Processing Units; Valkey serverless minimum 100 MB (from ~$6/month)
Cluster mode enabled shards up to 500 nodes; Multi-AZ with automatic failover; Global Datastore for cross-Region replicas
Memcached: multi-threaded, no replication or persistence
Caching patterns: lazy loading (cache-aside), write-through, TTLs to bound staleness
services.pricingModel: Node-based: per node-hour (Reserved Nodes / Database Savings Plans); Serverless: data stored GB-hours plus ECPUs; data transfer across AZs/Regions.

comparesWith.difference: MemoryDB persists writes to a Multi-AZ transaction log (durable primary DB); ElastiCache is a cache with optional snapshots.
DynamoDB with DAX gives microsecond reads for DynamoDB only; ElastiCache fronts any data source.

recentLaunches.title: Valkey 9.0 — up to 40% higher pipelined throughput, hash field expiration
Valkey 9.1 support for node-based clusters

interviewTips: Explain cache invalidation strategies and the thundering-herd problem
Recommend Valkey for cost and note migration from Redis OSS is in-place

services.name: Amazon MemoryDB
services.oneLiner: Durable, Valkey/Redis OSS-compatible in-memory database with a Multi-AZ transactional log for microsecond reads and single-digit-ms writes.
whenToUse: Primary database needing Redis data structures with durability (no data loss on failover)
Low-latency vector search in memory for real-time GenAI/semantic caching
whenNotToUse: Pure caching where durability is unnecessary (ElastiCache is cheaper)
Datasets far larger than affordable memory
keyFacts: Writes acknowledged after being persisted to a distributed Multi-AZ transaction log
Microsecond reads, single-digit-millisecond writes; up to 500 nodes per cluster
Multi-Region clusters (active-active) available for Valkey
Vector search supports millions of vectors with high recall at low latency
services.pricingModel: Per node-hour, per GB of data written, snapshot storage; reserved nodes and Database Savings Plans available.

comparesWith.difference: ElastiCache is a cache (can lose recent writes on failure); MemoryDB is durable.
DynamoDB is disk-based serverless with near-unlimited storage; MemoryDB keeps the full dataset in memory.

interviewTips: Use when the customer wants Redis as the system of record — ElastiCache replication is asynchronous

services.name: Amazon DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)
services.oneLiner: Managed JSON document database compatible with MongoDB APIs, built on Aurora-style distributed storage.
whenToUse: Migrating MongoDB workloads to a managed service with familiar drivers
Content management, catalogs and user profiles with flexible schemas
whenNotToUse: Apps relying on MongoDB features not supported by DocumentDB (check compatibility per version)
Very high-scale key-value access where DynamoDB is simpler and cheaper
keyFacts: Instance-based and elastic clusters (sharded); storage auto-scales to 128 TiB with 6 copies across 3 AZs
Up to 15 read replicas; Global Clusters for cross-Region DR with typically <1 s lag
Serverless option scales capacity automatically
MongoDB API compatibility 3.6, 4.0 and 5.0; supports vector search
services.pricingModel: Per instance-hour (or serverless capacity), storage per GB-month, I/O (Standard) or I/O-Optimized, backups; Database Savings Plans apply.

comparesWith.difference: DynamoDB is fully serverless key-value with its own API; DocumentDB offers MongoDB query language and indexes.

interviewTips: Mention compatibility testing and DMS for MongoDB migrations

services.name: Amazon Neptune
services.oneLiner: Managed graph database (Neptune Database) and in-memory graph analytics engine (Neptune Analytics) supporting Gremlin, openCypher and SPARQL.
whenToUse: Highly connected data: fraud rings, identity graphs, knowledge graphs, recommendations, network topology
GraphRAG with Bedrock Knowledge Bases (Neptune Analytics as vector + graph store)
whenNotToUse: Simple relationships that fit relational joins or key-value lookups
keyFacts: Neptune Database: up to 15 read replicas, storage up to 128 TiB replicated 6 ways across 3 AZs, Global Database support

Query languages: Apache TinkerPop Gremlin, openCypher, SPARQL 1.1 (RDF)
services.pricingModel: Per instance-hour or serverless NCU-hour, storage and I/O; Neptune Analytics per memory-optimized capacity unit-hour; Database Savings Plans cover Neptune Analytics (Mar 2026).

comparesWith.difference: DynamoDB can model adjacency lists but lacks graph traversal queries; Neptune executes multi-hop traversals natively.

recentLaunches.title: Database Savings Plans extended to Neptune Analytics and OpenSearch Service

interviewTips: Recognize graph-shaped questions ("friends of friends", "shared devices across accounts") and propose Neptune

services.name: Amazon Keyspaces (for Apache Cassandra)
services.oneLiner: Serverless, Cassandra Query Language (CQL)-compatible wide-column database.
whenToUse: Migrating Cassandra workloads without managing clusters
High-scale time-series/IoT style writes with CQL drivers
whenNotToUse: Greenfield apps with no Cassandra dependency (DynamoDB has richer integrations)
Workloads relying on unsupported Cassandra features (e.g. some UDFs/materialized views)
keyFacts: Data replicated 3 times across AZs; 99.99% SLA single-Region, 99.999% multi-Region
On-demand or provisioned capacity; multi-Region replication (active-active)
Max row size 1 MB; PITR up to 35 days
Table pre-warming sets throughput ahead of launches (Jan 2026)
services.pricingModel: Per read/write request unit (on-demand) or capacity unit-hour (provisioned), storage per GB-month, PITR and backups.

comparesWith.difference: DynamoDB uses its own API; Keyspaces keeps CQL compatibility for Cassandra apps.

recentLaunches.title: Table pre-warming for high-traffic launches

interviewTips: Position Keyspaces as the migration target for self-managed Cassandra operational pain

services.name: Amazon Timestream (for InfluxDB; LiveAnalytics closed to new customers)
services.oneLiner: Managed time-series databases: Timestream for InfluxDB is the recommended option; Timestream for LiveAnalytics has been closed to new customers since June 20, 2025.
whenToUse: IoT telemetry, DevOps metrics and industrial sensor data needing time-series queries (Timestream for InfluxDB)
Teams already using InfluxDB APIs/Telegraf/Grafana who want a managed service
whenNotToUse: New customers on Timestream for LiveAnalytics — it is in maintenance
Long-term analytical storage at PB scale (use S3 + Athena/Redshift)
keyFacts: Timestream for LiveAnalytics: no new customers from Jun 20, 2025; existing payer accounts can keep using it
Timestream for InfluxDB: single-instance or Multi-AZ, single-digit-ms query latency, InfluxDB 2.x/3 open-source APIs
IoT Core rule action can write directly to InfluxDB (Aug 2026)
services.pricingModel: Timestream for InfluxDB: per instance-hour by size plus provisioned storage; Database Savings Plans apply.

comparesWith.difference: DynamoDB can store time-series with TTL but lacks time-series functions; InfluxDB is purpose-built.
OpenSearch fits log/metric search and dashboards; Timestream for InfluxDB fits high-ingest numeric time series.

recentLaunches.title: Timestream for LiveAnalytics closed to new customers
AWS IoT Core rule action routes device data directly to InfluxDB

interviewTips: Show currency: recommend Timestream for InfluxDB, not LiveAnalytics, for new time-series designs

services.name: Amazon Redshift
services.oneLiner: Petabyte-scale columnar cloud data warehouse (provisioned RA3/RG or Serverless) with data sharing, zero-ETL and lakehouse queries.
whenToUse: BI and complex SQL analytics on structured/semi-structured data with high concurrency
Querying the S3 data lake (Spectrum/Iceberg) alongside warehouse tables; zero-ETL from Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB
Sharing live data across accounts/Regions without copies (data sharing)
whenNotToUse: OLTP with many small transactions (use Aurora/DynamoDB)
Occasional ad-hoc queries on S3 where Athena pay-per-query is cheaper
keyFacts: Columnar storage, MPP, zone maps; distribution styles (AUTO, EVEN, KEY, ALL) and sort keys
RA3 managed storage separates compute from storage; Redshift Serverless bills per RPU-hour with base capacity from 4 RPUs
Concurrency Scaling adds clusters for bursts (1 free hour/day credit per cluster); automatic WLM with query priorities
Graviton-based RG instances (May 2026) with integrated data lake query engine; Apache Iceberg v3 support (Aug 2026)
Automated snapshots (1–35 days) and cross-Region snapshot copy; Multi-AZ deployments for RA3
services.pricingModel: Provisioned: per node-hour (Reserved Instances) plus managed storage per GB-month; Serverless: per RPU-hour with per-second billing; Spectrum per TB scanned; Concurrency Scaling per second beyond free credits.

comparesWith.difference: Athena is serverless per-query SQL over S3 with no loading; Redshift delivers consistent performance for heavy, concurrent BI.
EMR runs Spark/Hadoop for flexible big-data processing; Redshift is a managed SQL warehouse.

recentLaunches.title: Significantly faster first-time (uncached) queries
Graviton-based RG instances with an integrated data lake query engine (up to 2.4x performance)
Apache Iceberg v3 table support

interviewTips: Explain distribution/sort key choices and how to avoid data skew and broadcast joins
Discuss zero-ETL vs DMS/Glue pipelines for operational analytics

services.name: Amazon VPC
services.oneLiner: Logically isolated Regional virtual network with subnets per AZ, route tables, gateways, security groups, NACLs and endpoints.
whenToUse: Every workload that needs private IP networking, segmentation and controlled internet/on-prem egress
Private access to AWS services via gateway endpoints (S3, DynamoDB) and interface endpoints (PrivateLink)
whenNotToUse: Connecting hundreds of VPCs with full-mesh peering — use Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN
keyFacts: Primary CIDR /16 to /28, up to 5 IPv4 CIDRs per VPC by default (adjustable); AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet

NAT gateway: up to 100 Gbps and 10 million pps; Regional NAT gateway (Nov 2025) spans AZs automatically and needs no public subnet
Gateway endpoints (S3/DynamoDB) are free; interface endpoints cost per AZ-hour plus per GB
VPC Encryption Controls (Nov 2025, priced from Mar 2026) audit and enforce encryption in transit within/across VPCs
Block Public Access for VPCs can centrally block IGW traffic; VPC Flow Logs capture accepted/rejected traffic metadata
services.pricingModel: VPC itself is free; pay for NAT gateways (hourly + per GB), public IPv4 addresses, interface endpoints, Flow Logs delivery, Traffic Mirroring, Encryption Controls, and cross-AZ/Region data transfer.

comparesWith.difference: TGW is a Regional hub with transitive routing for thousands of VPCs; VPC peering is 1:1 and non-transitive but has no per-GB processing fee.
VPC Lattice connects services (L7) across VPCs/accounts without network-level routing; VPC constructs route IP packets.

recentLaunches.title: Regional NAT gateway — single NAT that expands across AZs, no public subnet needed
VPC Encryption Controls enforce encryption in transit
AWS Management Console Private Access from VPCs without internet connectivity

interviewTips: Draw a 3-tier multi-AZ VPC: public subnets (ALB), private app subnets, isolated DB subnets; NAT per AZ (or Regional NAT)
Plan IP space for growth and non-overlap with on-prem; mention IPAM and IPv6 for EKS scale
Explain SG vs NACL troubleshooting (ephemeral ports for NACLs)

services.name: Amazon CloudFront
services.oneLiner: Global CDN with 600+ points of presence for caching, TLS termination, edge compute and DDoS/WAF protection — now with flat-rate plans.
whenToUse: Accelerating static and dynamic content, APIs and video globally
Protecting origins (S3 with OAC, ALB, custom) behind WAF and Shield at the edge
Edge logic with CloudFront Functions (sub-ms, viewer events) or Lambda@Edge (heavier, origin events)
whenNotToUse: Non-HTTP(S) TCP/UDP acceleration (use Global Accelerator)
Purely regional internal apps with no global audience
